Industry News: Open TTS Leaderboard: Scalable Evaluation for Multilingual Text-to-Speech and Voice Cloning

📅 30 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1389 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The pace of open-source text-to-speech (TTS) model releases has been incredible.
  • Evaluation, however, hasn't kept pace: it remains fragmented and unstandardized.
  • These arenas compare models by presenting owners with TTS outputs from two models, and asking them to choose one over the other.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The pace of open-source text-to-speech (TTS) model releases has been incredible. On the Hugging Face Hub (as of Sep 30, 2026) there are more than 8K TTS models available 🚀.

Evaluation, however, hasn't kept pace: it remains fragmented and unstandardized. The gold standard is human preference scores such as MOS or MUSHRA (more on metrics). To this end, several arena-based leaderboards have established themselves as useful reference points for the community:.

These arenas compare models by presenting owners with TTS outputs from two models, and asking them to choose one over the other. After collecting a sufficient number of votes, an Elo score is computed to rank models, typically with the Bradley–Terry model (see Voice Arena methodology).

While human preference is the ultimate decider, arenas cannot scale to keep up with the pace of TTS releases. This may partly explain why open-source models are underrepresented on arena-style leaderboards: as of Sep 30, 2026, only 16 of the 92 models on Artificial Analysis are open-weights, with a similar skew on Voice Arena. This likely reflects practical factors: adding an API model requires little more than an API key, whereas an open model must be hosted and served by the arena operator, and commercial providers have more reason to seek placement than open-source authors. Another limitation with arena-style evaluation is voter consistency: no arena can ensure that the same voters with the same criteria of “better” can consistently evaluate models over time. Even the preferences of a single person change over time (“A man cannot step into the same river twice” as famously remarked by Heraclitus).

To this end, we've built the Open TTS Leaderboard, which uses objective metrics to evaluate models on complementary aspects of performance:.

By relying on objective metrics evaluating a model drops from a couple weeks (for collecting votes) to a couple hours ⚡.

Importantly, the Open TTS Leaderboard does not replace human preference ranking. ASR-based WER provides a proxy for intelligibility, while speaker similarity estimates voice identity preservation. Neither directly measures naturalness, expressiveness, or listener preference. Nevertheless, they can even inform voting-based leaderboards which models to include in their evaluations.

Our intention with this leaderboard is for it to be shaped by the community; we want to hear your feedback so the evaluations stay relevant and insightful. The next few sections give an overview of main features of the Open TTS Leaderboard.

From the default view of the leaderboard, models are ranked by macro-average WER on the English splits of Seed TTS Eval (paper) and CV3 Eval (zero shot) (paper).

hexgrad/Kokoro-82M, Supertone/supertonic-3, and fishaudio/s2-pro lead the pack on English WER when averaged on these two splits, while the Pareto plots visualize which models strike a good balance between WER, batched inference (RTFx), and size.

Recent findings suggest that english performance doesn't necessarily translate to other languages. Multiple languages can be toggled to rank models on multilingual performance. Seed TTS Eval only has audio for English and Chinese, so the other languages are simply the score on CV3 Eval (zero shot). Note that Chinese, Japanese, and Korean are character-based languages and so character error rate (CER) is reported, and the “Average WER” across languages is a macro-average across languages.

k2-fsa/OmniVoice, fishaudio/s2-pro, and FunAudioLLM/Fun-CosyVoice3-0.5B-2512 are strong multilingual models.

By toggling “Voice cloning”, the models that support this functionality (on the selected languages) can be compared.

Moreover, a SIM column for speaker similarity now appears in the table, as well as two more Pareto plots for visualizing the tradeoff between SIM, batched inference, and size.

The average WER of some models, such as bosonai/higgs-tts-3-4b and openbmb/VoxCPM2, improve under voice cloning, namely when a reference audio is provided.

Industry observers note that numbers only tell part of the story, and as mentioned earlier human preference is the ultimate decider. From the “Listen” tab, you can compare the generated outputs that are behind the metrics, to find which model(s) you prefer!

Pick the language/dataset you're interested in, whether you want to compare voice cloning, and optionally pick the models or listen to outputs from a random selection.

The “Listen” tab fills an important gap in existing TTS leaderboards: a space to explore model outputs of various models.

In a recent development, you can even give feedback on the generated outputs. As we collect more votes from the community, we may include this data on the leaderboard. So vote! But please login with your HF account to help us weed out spam/bots.

In a recent development, the “Streaming” tab compares the streaming capabilities. Models are ranked by TTFA (time-to-first-audio), which quantifies how long a user waits after probing a model in order to obtain audio that can be played. This is important for voice agents and other interactive apps.

In a recent development, for streaming models (✅ under “Streaming API”) it's the time until the first audio chunk arrives. For non-streaming models, it's the time until the whole utterance is generated, because playback can't start any earlier. Every model runs one audio at a time (batch size 1), on the same 50 English prompts from CV3-Eval, on the same hardware and in its default voice. We drop the first 3 runs as warm-up and report the median TTFA across the rest.

The default view compares performance on an H200 GPU. Results are also available for CPU for a small (but growing) set of models!

kyutai/pocket-tts is a great model for streaming on both GPU and CPU!

Industry observers note that the goal of the Open TTS Leaderboard is not only to keep up with the incredible pace of TTS model releases, but to be shaped by the community; we want to hear your feedback so the evaluations stay relevant and insightful. Let us know which datasets, models, and metrics you want to see!

We will soon open-source the evaluation scripts, much like the Open ASR Leaderboard repo, so that you can directly provide your feedback and suggestions via GitHub Problems and PRs! Let's shape TTS evaluations together 🤗.

Glad this board splits multilingual TTS quality from voice-cloning identity instead of one aggregate green.

According to recent reports, the check I'd keep reading: whether the ranking still holds when you hold language/domain fixed versus when cloning is the axis. Otherwise teams optimize the easier subscale and still call the result "SOTA TTS.".

In a recent development, english performance doesn't necessarily translate to other languages. Multiple languages can be toggled to rank models on multilingual performance. Seed TTS Eval only has movie box audio for English and Chinese, so the other languages are simply the score on CV3 Eval (zero shot). Note that Chinese, Japanese, and Korean are character-based languages and so character error rate (CER) is reported, and the “Average WER” across languages is a macro-average across languages.

Open TTS Leaderboard is an open evaluation platform designed to make multilingual text-to-speech and voice-cloning models easier to compare at scale. Traditional TTS arenas usually let consumers listen to outputs from two models and choose the one they prefer. Those votes can then be used to calculate an Elo-style score, often through approaches such as the Bradley–Terry model, giving users a simple way to understand how different systems perform based on human preference.

It has been revealed that human feedback remains an important part of evaluating speech quality, but relying only on arena-style voting can be difficult as new TTS models are released at a rapid pace. Open-source models can also face practical barriers because they generally need to be hosted and served by the evaluation platform, while API-based commercial models can be added more easily. This can result in open-weight systems being less visible on public leaderboards. Another challenge is consistency: people's preferences and listening criteria can change over time, meaning that votes collected months apart may not always represent exactly the same standards.

Industry observers note that open TTS Leaderboard aims to address these challenges by providing a scalable and transparent space for evaluating multilingual TTS and voice-cloning systems. The goal is to make comparisons easier to reproduce, expand coverage of open models, and provide useful evaluation signals alongside human preference. By bringing together scalable testing and community feedback, the project can help researchers, developers, and users better understand how speech models perform across different languages, voices, and use cases.

GitHub repo with the eval scripts is public! https://github.com/huggingface/open-tts-leaderboard.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The final talk at Kangrejos 2026 was about the removal of the C implementation of Android's Binder driver, the primary interprocess communication mechanism used on Android devices.
  • Binder was added to the kernel in 2008, Llamas noted, as an interprocess communication mechanism for Android devices.
  • That made it an obvious candidate for porting to Rust, Llamas stated.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The final talk at Kangrejos 2026 was about the removal of the C implementation of Android's Binder driver, the primary interprocess communication mechanism used on Android devices. Carlos Llamas revealed that he had deleted the C code to general applause, and then shared some insights about what went into replacing the C implementation. Alice Ryhl, who has worked on the Rust implementation for some years, added her own thoughts about what the most difficult and interesting parts of the transition were.

Binder was added to the kernel in 2008, Llamas noted, as an interprocess communication mechanism for Android devices. Its design originated in BeOS, but it has grown significantly since then. It provides a rich set of operations for allowing processes to communicate with the minimum amount of overhead. It also, therefore, presents a large attack surface for Android. Many complicated chained attacks against Android have involved Binder at one step or another, Llamas explained. Google's internal "red team" (the team dedicated to proactive security research) deemed Binder to be the most vulnerability-dense component in the entire operating system, with more CVEs per line than anywhere else.

That made it an obvious candidate for porting to Rust, Llamas stated. Binder was the first user of Rust in the kernel, he added, although Ryhl did not publicly post the first version of what became the Rust implementation until 2023, well after the Rust experiment started in 2021. All told, the effort took more than five years. Binder is used for every single screen touch, permission check, and cross-application message on Android, which runs on more than three billion devices. In total, it works out to hundreds of billions of Binder transactions per second, globally, he added. That scale meant that even the smallest discrepancy between the interface provided by the C version and the one provided by the Rust version would cause problems and regressions for some use case.

Sources indicate that one particularly tricky aspect has been performance, Ryhl said. Throughput doesn't matter that much; what matters is the tail latencies. Most screen frames on Android have a Binder transaction in the critical path of the frame, she explained. So, a difference of two microseconds on average is not a real problem, but if Binder is ever twenty milliseconds slower, even once in a while, people will notice and care.

It has been revealed that the actual algorithms that the C and Rust implementations use are identical, she continued, so there are no large differences in throughput. But, because Rust handles locking differently, there were problems with the tail latency from lock contention that she had to debug. For example, one user-reported traceback showed Binder attempting to take a mutex that was held by another process. That process was preempted, and did not resume executing for twenty milliseconds, well past the sixteen millisecond budget to render a single frame.

In a recent development, it was a classic case of priority inversion. To solve the problem in Binder, Ryhl moved as many operations out from under the lock as possible, and was able to replace it with a spinlock, which made the problem go away. The equivalent lock in the C implementation was already a spinlock: "I deviated from C Binder, and pow. It has eighteen years of accumulated quirks.".

Eventually, however, the Rust implementation was good enough for most use cases. And the C implementation was still producing new vulnerabilities every time someone tried to introduce a new feature. Eventually, Llamas and Ryhl decided to only add new features to the Rust implementation, in order to motivate people to switch and to avoid headaches from the C implementation. That policy has resulted in the Rust version becoming faster than the C version, because Ryhl was able to introduce an algorithmic improvement that reduced the number of needed system calls, a change that had been considered too complex for the C implementation. Now that the C implementation has been deleted, there are more of those coming, she promised.

Recent findings suggest that another area that proved difficult was dealing with tracepoints. Consumers aren't supposed to rely on the presence or behavior of most kernel-internal tracepoints, but they do. This meant that Ryhl had to copy the existing tracepoints in Binder as a de facto part of the driver's API. That even extended into some of the data structures involved in the driver. In one case, she said, there was a reference-counted structure that had a slightly different reference count in the Rust implementation, because the Rust code was holding an additional pointer to the structure. That turned out to be a problem for one particular piece of client code, since it relied on checking the reference count via a tracepoint in order to determine when the C implementation had reached a particular state.

In a recent development, there was also a lot of toolchain support needed, Ryhl continued. The Rust implementation had to work with kernel address-space layout randomization (KASLR), control-flow integrity (CFI), and profile-guided optimization. Production Android kernels are built with all of those enabled, and since they impact code generation, the Rust code needed to account for them.

Sources indicate that llamas then went into more detail about the deployment proposal that will be used to convert consumers to the Rust implementation. A major problem with just rolling the Rust implementation out is the existence of vendor hooks: custom tracepoints used to inject vendor-specific behavior into the kernel. The Rust implementation of Binder was not able to reproduce those in every case, and therefore many vendors are stuck on the C implementation until they update their code. That's going to be a slow process.

According to recent reports, old stable versions of the kernel will continue to have the C Binder, and receive security fixes, which gives the various Android vendors a little bit of leeway until they're forced to update. After the conference, the patch removing the C implementation was merged as part of the 7.4 merge window, so that is the version past which the Rust implementation is required. 7.3 is the designated long-term-support release for 2026.

In a recent development, one person asked whether this would pose a problem for people compiling the kernel with GCC. Miguel Ojeda responded that many distributions are using a workaround for the current lack of Rust support in GCC: they are building the C side of the kernel with GCC, and the Rust side with LLVM. He stated that he had advised against compiling the kernel in that way, because it is "a complete hack", though people who use it are unlikely to complain about being forced onto Clang. Greg Kroah-Hartman added that it will take months or years to learn about anyone who has problems with the Rust version of the driver, given how slowly Android vendors upgrade their kernels. Furthermore, the removal is a single patch that can be cleanly reverted, if someone needs to continue using the C version.

Sources indicate that llamas thought that it was worth considering what the removal process should look like for other code that gets ported to Rust. He asked what people thought should happen to the C version of converted drivers on long-term-support branches. Ojeda mentioned that the process would be exactly the same as the existing policy for replaced C code. The only difference between Rust and C in long-term-support releases is that the Rust maintainers backport fixes for soundness problems, he said. Kroah-Hartman told Llamas not to worry about code that has been replaced: "Just delete it. I take patches for subsystems that have been deleted. It's fine.".

With that declaration, the session, the conference, and the presence of the C Binder driver in the kernel were all over. Binder is the first nontrivial component in the kernel to be ported to Rust, and its journey has revealed several pitfalls that don't apply to upcoming drivers written in Rust from scratch. Still, the most difficult problems were not Rust-specific; they were the compatibility problems that any rewrite would face. Whether any other kernel components will find the hassle of a rewrite worth it, and how long they will take to accomplish it, remains to be seen.

Sources indicate that san Francisco, Calif. — On Friday, November 20, workers at Internet Archive announced their intent to form a union with the Communications Workers of America (CWA). They are seeking to join CWA Local 9415 in Oakland, California.

In a letter sent this morning via email, members of the union’s organizing committee presented management with a request for voluntary recognition after a supermajority of eligible workers signed cards signaling their desires for union representation. Worker-organizers for the union have also simultaneously filed a petition for a union certification election with the National Labor Relations Board (NLRB); if Internet Archive grants the union’s request for voluntary recognition, organizers will withdraw the NLRB petition.

In a recent development, “We are forming a union because we care deeply about the Internet Archive, its patrons, and its place as a vital part of the internet ecosystem. Now more than ever, we want the Internet Archive to last for the generations to come,” remarked organizing committee member Danielle Leard, a digitization technician for the Internet Archive. “Sustaining workers long-term, through job security, livable wages, and sufficient benefits, goes hand-in-hand with sustaining the Archive long-term.”.

“Throughout the years, many of us have witnessed the significant extent to which the Internet Archive and its patrons benefit from some of the most talented, dedicated, and overall purpose-driven folks that we’ve had the privilege of working alongside,” remarked organizing committee member Chelsea Richelle Smith, a patron services specialist at Internet Archive. “At its core, we all share the collective desire to foster a workplace in which everyone thrives. We believe in continuing to build towards a democratic environment where the workers have a meaningful voice in the work that we do and the conditions under which that work is done, in alignment with each other and the organization’s overall mission.”.

The Internet Archive is one of the world’s largest and oldest libraries of digitized media, with nearly 120 librarians, engineers, technicians, project managers, media specialists, facilities workers, and administrative staff making up the proposed unit. Together, Internet Archive workers ensure that the Archive remains a beacon of equitable knowledge to millions of customers worldwide through several different services, such as the Wayback Machine, Open Library, and most recently, the digital preservation of government documents.

“In solidarity with workers across the country, we aim to model the practice of workplace democracy and the building of technology that benefits the public,” said organizing committee member Will Howes, an engineer on the Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine. “We organized the Internet Archive not only for each other as coworkers, but to show the tech and non-profit sectors what is possible. Any worker can and should believe that talking to their colleagues today is the first step towards improving their workplace conditions.”.

The union’s announcement marks the latest effort to democratize universal and free access to knowledge; in September, U.S.-based Wikimedia Foundation workers secured union recognition with CWA, and in the union’s vision statement, worker organizers cited the successful unionization efforts at the Free Software Foundation (FSF) and the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) as inspirations for organizing.

In a recent development, “In a rapidly evolving technology landscape, collective action and strong workplace protections help ensure that workers are heard and respected,” stated CWA Local 9415 President Decovan Rhem. “We are proud to stand strong with the Internet Archive workers to obtain union recognition and advocate for a positive, inclusive workplace.”.

The union has launched a petition to garner public support for voluntary recognition. For more updates, follow Internet Archive Labor Union-CWA Local 9415 (IALU-CWA) on Bluesky, Instagram, Mastodon, and Tumblr.

The Campaign to Organize Digital Employees (CODE-CWA) is a network of worker-organizers and their staff working every single day to build the voice and power necessary to ensure the future of the tech, game, and digital industries in the United States and Canada. CODE-CWA is a project of the Communications Workers of America, which represents hundreds of thousands of workers throughout tech, media, telecom, and other industries who stand together to fight for justice on the job and in our communities.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, the optional KB5132057 update arrived on November 19, after this month's Patch Tuesday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Windows Search gets a makeover, while Hello lights up dim rooms.

Microsoft has delivered its final scheduled non-security preview update of 2026 for Windows 11 25H2 and 26H2, with an updated Windows Search experience and a brighter Windows Hello for users who prefer darker rooms.

According to recent reports, the optional KB5132057 update arrived on November 19, after this month's Patch Tuesday. Microsoft is skipping December's non-security preview because of reduced holiday operations, though that doesn't cancel the monthly security release. This last preview is quite a doozy.

Industry observers note that the big-ticket item is the "fresh Windows Search Experience." We saw a preview of this last month, and Microsoft has gone well beyond the "just make it work" request of many Windows users. Results appear faster with less clutter, the tool uses memory better, and files can be previewed directly in Windows Search.

We're less convinced by inline actions, which let consumers perform common tasks directly through Windows Search without opening Settings. In our testing, "turn on dark mode" worked, but "switch on dark mode" did not, thus highlighting the limitations of the tool. In addition, we remain unconvinced that Windows Search is the place to run actions.

That remarked, anything that makes Windows Search less of a punchline for unkind jokes about performance and accuracy is welcome, as are other features, including an optional screen-brightening feature for Windows Hello facial recognition in dim rooms, and the PowerToys-esque Run dialog, which consumers can enable in Settings.

While some of the new features won't be enabled immediately, Microsoft has included fixes that will be available right away. One addresses an glitch where Windows Fax and Scan could fail to connect to a fax server. Handy for those occasions when email falls over into a heap.

There are also fixes for Windows IoT Enterprise LTSC activation failures and the misleading "Something went wrong" message shown on Android devices during cross-device passkey authentication. At the time of writing, Microsoft still lists the problem as something for which "we are working on a resolution to be released in a future Windows upgrade.".

Sadly, not everything has been pushed off the naughty step. SQL Server queries using OLE DB providers can still leave connections to external databases open after they've finished. Microsoft is working on that one and "will provide an revision in an upcoming release." ®.

#115323. AutoSynthData: Generating Training Data for Enterprise Agents

AutoSynthData: Generating Training Data for Enterprise Agents

📅 02 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2028 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Enterprises need agents that work well in their own environments.
  • The difficulty is turning those weaknesses into training data.
  • At ServiceNow CoreAI, we built AutoSynthData to turn those capability gaps into training data.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Enterprises need agents that work well in their own environments. The work they ask these agents to do is shaped by the systems they use, the rules they follow, and the state of their data. A model may be broadly capable and still struggle with a particular environment: a workflow it handles poorly, a combination of tools it misuses, or a constraint it fails to respect. Those are the weaknesses an enterprise needs to improve.

The difficulty is turning those weaknesses into training data. An individual failure tells us something, but training a model requires many fresh tasks that exercise the same capability in different situations. Those tasks must also be possible to complete in the environment, resemble work someone would actually request, and have a reliable way to check whether the agent succeeded.

At ServiceNow CoreAI, we built AutoSynthData to turn those capability gaps into training data. It uses a target model’s failures and a stronger teacher’s successes to decide what the model should learn next, then generates and validates new tasks that exercise those capabilities. As the model improves, the curriculum shifts toward what it still finds difficult. We illustrate the pipeline with EnterpriseOps Gym (Malay et al., 2026), using the released dataset. We begin by describing the environment an agent operates in and what makes a task useful for training.

An agentic environment defines the world in which an agent operates: the state it can observe and modify, the tools and APIs it can invoke, and the state transitions produced by its actions.

According to recent reports, A task is instantiated within this environment. We use the following abstraction:.

The system specification defines the constraints under which the agent operates, including system instructions, environment policies, and, when applicable, task-specific initialization such as a seeded database state or a set of knowledge articles.

Recent findings suggest that the specification must be compatible with the environment’s tools, state, and supported actions. Its instructions should be clear and avoid arbitrary constraints introduced solely to manufacture difficulty.

The user prompt specifies what the user wants the agent to accomplish, together with any user-level constraints. A generated task should satisfy three properties.

Feasibility. There should exist at least one trajectory in the current environment that satisfies the user prompt while respecting the system specification. This rules out tasks that depend on unavailable tools, inaccessible knowledge, impossible state transitions, or actions prohibited by policy.

Realism. The user prompt should resemble something a user would plausibly ask in the target environment. The space of executable behaviors is usually much larger than the space of realistic workflows.

According to recent reports, difficulty. For training, the task should expose a weakness of the current agent. Tasks that are already solved reliably provide little newly introduced training signal. The useful region is therefore tasks that are feasible and realistic, but not yet consistently solved.

Sources indicate that the verifier determines whether the resulting trajectory successfully completes the task. It should satisfy three properties.

Consistency. It should agree with the user prompt, the system specification, and the task-specific environment state.

Soundness. It should reject trajectories that fail to satisfy the task or violate relevant constraints.

Industry observers note that completeness. It should accept valid solutions rather than encode one particular reference trajectory.

These properties matter directly during training. A lax verifier can reward incorrect behavior, while an overly restrictive verifier can penalize valid solutions.

Industry observers note that given an environment and a target model, AutoSynthData generates training tasks consisting of a system specification, user prompt, and verifier. The generated tasks are grounded in the environment and selected to provide useful training signal for the current model.

Industry observers note that autoSynthData first evaluates the target model in the environment using diagnostic tasks and identifies patterns in the tasks it struggles to complete. A stronger teacher helps characterize which of those tasks are solvable and what successful behavior looks like. AutoSynthData turns the resulting capability gaps into fresh executable tasks, checks each task in the environment, and uses accepted samples for post-training. Evaluating the updated model reveals which gaps remain and can guide the next round of generation.

Recent findings suggest that autoSynthData uses evaluation runs in the target environment to identify what the model needs to learn next. In our EnterpriseOps Gym experiment, we run both the target model and a stronger teacher on the evaluation tasks. We examine those runs to identify:.

We distill these findings into sanitized capability specification cards. The evaluation tasks guide what the model should learn, but the generator does not receive their original prompts, entities, trajectories, or verifier details. It receives the cards and uses them to create latest tasks with different prompts, states, and solution paths.

Sources indicate that identifying a capability gap tells us what to teach, but training requires many varied tasks that exercise it. AutoSynthData uses the specification card to generate those tasks.

Suppose the target model struggles with tasks that require the following workflow:.

The generator creates new tasks that exercise this workflow, varying the entities, initial environment state, workflow composition, tool combinations, wording, and difficulty. The stronger teacher then demonstrates a successful trajectory for each task. For supervised fine-tuning (SFT), these demonstrations teach the target model how to apply the capability in new situations.

AutoSynthData builds the dataset in two phases: first generating and validating core samples, then expanding them into novel variants.

Industry observers note that the target phase creates the core set of training samples from the capability specifications. Workers generate independent tasks in parallel, picking up a new target when they finish. Each candidate goes through validation, execution, solver evaluation, and repair before acceptance. The result is a batch of vetted examples built around what the target model needs to learn.

The multiply phase expands the dataset by creating novel variants of accepted target samples. Each variant has its own user request, environment state, entity configuration, reference trajectory, and verifier, and must pass the same validation and execution checks. A multiplied sample cannot seed another multiplied sample. This anchors expansion to the vetted target set and limits drift across generations.

It has been revealed that to support both phases, AutoSynthData separates generation control from environment-specific execution. A shared controller coordinates generation, quality control, coverage, and dataset construction, while an adapter handles environment execution, task and state management, reference replay, deterministic verification, solver execution, and task profiling.

According to recent reports, together, parallel target generation and multiplication provide a path to training-scale datasets. Their usefulness depends on the checks applied to every candidate: the task must be executable, the solution must work, and the verifier must distinguish success from failure.

It has been revealed that generating a plausible request is not enough to produce useful training data. A task may be impossible in the target environment, its reference solution may fail when executed, or its verifier may reward the wrong final state. AutoSynthData checks these properties before accepting a task for training.

AutoSynthData reviews quality at two levels: individual candidates must pass verification, and batches must provide useful coverage and diversity.

According to recent reports, each candidate must clear a quality-control loop before entering the training dataset. We begin with solver evaluation to measure difficulty. In the configuration used here, we favor tasks the target model solves on no more than one of three trials and the stronger solver solves on at least two of three trials. Candidates also undergo positive and negative verification and a bounded repair process.

The positive gate asks: Does the intended solution solve the generated task?

The pipeline executes the reference trajectory in the target environment and checks the resulting state against the candidate’s verifier. This reveals mismatches among the prompt, initial state, solution, and success criteria.

The negative gate asks: Do relevant incorrect outcomes fail?

It has been revealed that for example, it can mutate parts of the expected outcome and confirm that those states no longer pass verification. This catches weak verifiers that award success without requiring the intended behavior.

Failed candidates go to a critic before being discarded. The critic examines the sample and its failure, looking for inconsistent state, impossible workflows, incorrect task construction, bad reference trajectories, weak verifier logic, or a mismatch with the intended capability. The critic’s findings guide repairs, with a fixed limit on retries:.

In a recent development, A repaired task must pass the relevant checks again. The diagnosis guides repairs to the existing candidate rather than requiring generation to start over.

Passing these checks makes a sample eligible for training, but individually valid samples can still form a repetitive or unbalanced dataset. AutoSynthData therefore also reviews generation at the batch level.

A batch may overrepresent a few easy task families, miss a capability, or reflect too much generation effort spent on a low-yield pattern.

In a recent development, A meta-review examines accepted samples, rejected samples, and generation behavior across each batch. It asks:.

The controller tracks coverage in the accepted dataset, reduces generation in overrepresented regions, and directs more work toward gaps. When a region repeatedly produces poor candidates, critiques and meta-review guide changes to the generation strategy. These adjustments balance useful learning signal, task quality, coverage, diversity, and low redundancy within the available generation budget and dataset size requirements.

Together, these feedback loops improve both individual tasks and the dataset they form: sample-level checks guide candidate repair, while batch-level review guides future generation.

Sources indicate that the useful training distribution changes as the model improves. AutoSynthData treats synthetic data generation as a search for tasks near the target model's capability boundary: difficult enough to expose weaknesses, but solvable enough for the teacher to provide reliable demonstrations.

Recent findings suggest that after post-training, we evaluate the updated model in the same environment. Tasks it now solves reliably are less useful for the next training round; persistent failures point to capabilities that still need attention. Those results can guide the next generation round.

It has been revealed that our experiments focus on SFT, but the same mechanism could support reinforcement learning (RL): generate tasks that challenge the current policy and provide reliable learning signal, train, then move the generation target with the updated policy. We blueprint to test this moving, difficulty-calibrated frontier beyond SFT.

We use EnterpriseOps Gym to test whether this approach improves a model on tasks in a stateful enterprise environment. We generate training tasks in the Gym’s Hybrid and ITSM environments, fine-tune the target model on accepted samples, and evaluate the resulting checkpoints.

We tested the pipeline on the Hybrid domain of EnterpriseOps Gym using Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it as the target model and Qwen3.8-27B as the teacher.

Industry observers note that autoSynthData generated 2,000 synthetic training samples in about 18 hours. We fine-tuned Gemma on this dataset and evaluated the resulting checkpoints on the benchmark. The best checkpoint was epoch 5.

The synthetic SFT checkpoint improves mean Pass@1 by 7.2 percentage points, a 35% relative improvement, and raises verifier success from 63.01% to 68.55%. It closes 59% of the original Pass@1 gap between Gemma and the reference model.

Industry observers note that the training tasks were newly generated from capability specifications; the generator did not receive the original evaluation tasks. The result demonstrates improvement in EnterpriseOps Gym Hybrid, the environment used for this experiment.

We also applied AutoSynthData to the ITSM domain of EnterpriseOps Gym, using Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it as the target model and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash as the teacher. AutoSynthData generated 1,994 synthetic training samples in 66 hours. Generation took longer than in the subsequent Hybrid run described above, primarily because the ITSM run used a larger teacher model and preceded pipeline optimizations that improved throughput.

On ITSM, synthetic SFT raises mean Pass@1 from 18.77% to 27.18%, showing that the approach also improves performance in a second domain.

The tasks most useful for training depend on both the environment and the model working in it. AutoSynthData uses the model’s failures to choose what to generate, validates new tasks against the environment, and makes those tasks available for post-training. Our EnterpriseOps Gym results show the value of that approach in a controlled setting. As the model changes, the same process can focus on the gaps that remain.

AI boom threatens circuit board crunch to rival pandemic-era chip shortage

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (671 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Trade body warns automotive, medical, and defense orders are being crowded out, with relief unlikely before mid-2028.
  • The electronics industry faces a printed circuit board (PCB) shortage that could rival the pandemic-era chip crunch – with AI once again accused of hogging supplies.
  • The Global Electronics Association states demand is arriving "at a scale the supply chain was not built for," straining everything from glass fabric and resin to finished boards.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Trade body warns automotive, medical, and defense orders are being crowded out, with relief unlikely before mid-2028.

The electronics industry faces a printed circuit board (PCB) shortage that could rival the pandemic-era chip crunch – with AI once again accused of hogging supplies.

The Global Electronics Association states demand is arriving "at a scale the supply chain was not built for," straining everything from glass fabric and resin to finished boards.

Recent findings suggest that its report, "The PCB Squeeze: A Wake-Up Call for Global Electronics," claims AI servers need increasingly complex boards. While a typical PC board has about 12 layers of tracks, AI server boards can have 40 to 60 layers or more, and each additional layer requires more resin, copper foil, and laminate.

The supply of materials is set to be constrained through at least the first half of 2027, the report states, with meaningful relief unlikely before mid-2028.

Programs to deliver PCBs for automotive, industrial, medical and even the defense industries are being crowded out as AI soaks up scarce capacity, it claims.

Sources indicate that the association's North American figures show orders growing much faster than deliveries. PCB bookings rose 56.1 percent in the first nine months of 2026 compared with the same period last year, while PCB shipments increased 13.3 percent.

Fabrication capacity is expanding, aimed at meeting the increased demand from the AI infrastructure sector, especially in Asia, where more than 90 percent of the world's boards are made. The report states that $10 billion has gone toward upcoming PCB plants in Southeast Asia, and at least as much has been invested in China over the past three years, but the raw materials are themselves constrained.

According to recent reports, it warns of lengthening lead times for those raw materials. Standard FR-4 laminate now takes six to eight weeks to ship, up from two to three weeks a year ago, while advanced low-loss laminates now take 14 to 18 weeks for delivery, for example.

Tightening supplies usually lead to price increases, and the report indicates that suppliers raised laminate costs by 30 percent in September, and that the price tag of some types of E-glass cloth for circuit boards has risen by 300 percent.

It has been revealed that the report also puts copper prices up 37 percent over the past year. Concerns have been raised about copper supplies before, as The Register has reported multiple times.

The association compares the risk with the 2021 chip shortage, when disrupted supplies left manufacturers unable to secure even relatively mundane components.

New capacity is coming, but it is late and comes in dribs and drabs, according to the report, while AI demand just keeps on absorbing it as soon as it arrives.

It has been revealed that the association's advice is for buyers to plan early, and to share realistic forecasts with suppliers rather than double-booking. Board makers should qualify alternative suppliers of materials such as laminate and copper foil before shortages bite, but it warns against stockpiling beyond real need, which adds to forward-buying pressure.

But it would like governments to step in, of course, by tracking board and material lead times with industry and offering tax incentives for investment in advanced PCB and substrate manufacturing equipment.

Recent findings suggest that the wish list also includes state investment in research and development plus qualification of new alternative materials. It would like to see loan guarantees and grants to protect critical programs and small fabricators, structured so as to sustain new capacity if forward buying unravels and demand corrects in 2027.

"Yes, we are seeing constraint in upstream materials and have been reporting it for the past couple of quarters," said Cori Masters, senior research analyst director for Supply Chain Operations at Gartner.

According to recent reports, "In addition, AI datacenter infrastructure build out is moving capacity support to high-layer count PCBs which increase throughput time and decreases availability of line utilization for more traditional PCB products," she told The Register. ®.

Announcing jj-musubi: live sync for Jujutsu

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (859 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Serpentine

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that I’m pleased to announce a new source control tool, jj-musubi, that live-syncs copies of a Jujutsu (jj) repository across multiple machines.
  • jj-musubi makes repos on multiple machines feel like jj workspaces (worktrees if you speak git).
  • It’s intended for use by one person who works across several machines, so it has no security model (or rather, that is the extent of its security model).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that I’m pleased to announce a new source control tool, jj-musubi, that live-syncs copies of a Jujutsu (jj) repository across multiple machines. Every time jj snapshots my work, jj-musubi syncs it to every machine in moments, and also commits, rebases, fetches, and so on.

This simple capability is surprisingly powerful.

jj-musubi makes repos on multiple machines feel like jj workspaces (worktrees if you speak git).

It’s intended for use by one person who works across several machines, so it has no security model (or rather, that is the extent of its security model).

Recent findings suggest that jujutsu already treats the working copy as a commit. Running jj status records a snapshot of my edits in that commit, which jj-musubi then syncs to my other machines. I like to have my shell prompt run jj status, so in practice I rarely have to think about snapshots.

It has been revealed that jj-musubi does not write to the working copy. Each machine has its own working copy and workspaces as usual, so syncs of commits, snapshots, and rewrites can bring in new history while a build is running, without changing the files under it. On a laptop, I can work offline, and my machine will sync when I’m back on the network.

Sources indicate that this has also proven handy when I have agents working on several machines. I can give each agent its own jj workspace on different systems, then run jj diff -r devbox/agent-1@ on the laptop to see what one of them has done so far. If one finds a bug that another needs to fix, they can coordinate and see each other’s work without overhead.

jj-musubi refers to a collection of copies of a repo as a hive.

Recent findings suggest that I often run agents in temporary disposable VMs. jj-musubi supports this by allowing an agent to lease its repo’s membership in the hive: if it doesn’t renew that lease in time, its repo gets forgotten about, so temporary repos or vanished containers can’t just stack up and clutter things.

In a recent development, back when I was at Meta, I kicked off the project that became Sapling and Mononoke. Sapling’s Commit Cloud gives engineers there a similar way to move work between machines, and Google engineers have something similar with an internal jj server.

Since then, I’d missed that everyday convenience for the machines I already use, and felt like I could get it without massive infrastructure or hosting. With jj-musubi, one machine runs a hub, and daemons exchange jj history with it over SSH. That’s almost as lightweight as you can get.

Recent findings suggest that what’s tricky is getting concurrent work right. That’s already hard in any distributed source control system, and when syncs are live and we initiative for disconnected work in an unreliable network, the difficulty goes way up.

As a user, I shouldn’t have to care about when exactly I can safely close my laptop after finishing an edit; all of my changes should make it through either just before I close it, or right after I reopen. No work should get lost or corrupted in the presence of interrupts, resends, delays, or machines sleeping, and the system should stay reliable even when machines go offline forever.

I used Lean to prove key properties of jj-musubi’s network protocol, and tests compare the Rust code against that model. An extensive body of other tests run real jj repositories through concurrent edits, interrupted syncs, hub restarts, and a myriad of other nasty situations. Mutation and adversarial testing ensure that when bugs are injected, sensible things happen. The safety guide details all the checks (and the parts I don’t yet cover).

It might sound spooky or dangerous to be able to see in-progress work on one machine from another. How can that be safe?

Recent findings suggest that if you use jj in multiple workspaces, you’re already used to the novelty of being able to check out the same change in two workspaces and modify it. jj simply marks the change as divergent, but it won’t patch either working copy with changes from the other until you decide to, e.g. by calling jj workspace update-stale. In jj, dealing with divergent versions of a change is similar to any other kind of conflicted merge.

jj-musubi uses jj’s existing workspace machinery, so everything will feel familiar. The only difference is that when you run jj-musubi, a workspace’s name is prefixed with the name of the machine it lives on.

Start with e.g. a laptop and another machine that’s always on (let’s call it devbox), with a copy of a jj repo on each. On each machine, download the binary or build it yourself:.

Run musubi hub on devbox; it will keep your sync data in ~/musubi-hub. In the laptop’s repo, run musubi create --hub devbox. In devbox’s repo, run musubi join.

Sources indicate that I provide builds for Linux, macOS and Windows, and the quick start walks through setup and the first sync. If you try it and something surprises you, I’d like to hear about it.

The Agent Said It Was Done. The Database Disagreed.

📅 03 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2599 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, microsoft ThinkingBox grades AI agents on the records they leave behind, not the sentences they generate, and then asks whether they can do it twenty times in a row.
  • Figure 1: ThinkingBox runs an agent against isolated MCP tool sessions, then grades the terminal backend state and side effects it leaves behind.
  • Her $745 kitchen appliance has been stuck in a courier "exception" at a Nashville distribution center, fifteen days past its estimated delivery date.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, microsoft ThinkingBox grades AI agents on the records they leave behind, not the sentences they generate, and then asks whether they can do it twenty times in a row. It is now available through Hugging Face.

Figure 1: ThinkingBox runs an agent against isolated MCP tool sessions, then grades the terminal backend state and side effects it leaves behind. From our ThinkingBox paper.

A customer writes in. Her $745 kitchen appliance has been stuck in a courier "exception" at a Nashville distribution center, fifteen days past its estimated delivery date.

The AI agent does careful work. Nine tool calls: it pulls the order, checks tracking, looks up her customer profile, searches the refund policy twice, confirms no ticket exists, opens one, documents the timeline, and reads the policy correctly; her account segment genuinely does not qualify for late-delivery compensation.

It has been revealed that then it closes the ticket as resolved and replies “ Since your query is resolved, is there anything I may assist you with? ”.

According to recent reports, two things are wrong. The carrier exception is still open, so the required end state was on hold, pending resolution. And the customer never got a real answer to what she actually asked.

An AI grader checking tool calls would see nine well-formed ones. The grader checking whether the agent wrote to the database would see that too. The database is what disagrees.

That gap is what ThinkingBox measures. Across 507 stateful business workflows, each run 20 times against various LLM models, it grades agents on terminal backend state and side effects. This post covers what we found, what consistency costs, and how to run the benchmark yourself through OpenEnv.

In a recent development, you can run this one yourself: the example above is adapted from a benchmark task sandbox_external_retail_group1.py:test_case_ST003_006, and the executable check that fails is a single field: the ticket's status is solved where the required end state is hold. The full trace is in Appendix D.4, Case 3 of our paper.

Want to try it before reading the results? Skip to section Run it yourself.

Final responses and valid tool calls are only proxies. An agent can sound correct while leaving the wrong value, changing the wrong record, or creating an extra side effect. Only the records it leaves behind settle the question.

The gap is substantial. In a common-set ablation covering 121,680 valid trials across 12 LLM models, 79,853 attempts failed the executable checks. Of those failures, 67.24% still terminated cleanly, invoked a state-changing tool, and reported no final tool error. Executable checks nevertheless found wrong field values in 77.61% of them, unintended extra effects in 43.30%, and missing required effects in 25.36%. Those state-check findings overlap.

A trajectory is a claim. Database state is the evidence. Repetition is the trust test.

An agent that processes a refund correctly once and mishandles it the next four times is not a working refund agent. So every task runs 20 independent times, each from an identical clean backend, and we report three different things:.

Table 1: The three numbers we report, and the question each one answers.

Sources indicate that we use observed 20/20 in this blog post as the literal count of how many of the 507 tasks passed 20 out of 20. No estimator, no smoothing.

In a recent development, starting with the familiar view. The table below reports pass@1, the single-attempt score estimate, broken out by domain. This is the number most leaderboards publish, and on its own it reads like an ordinary capability ranking.

Sources indicate that table 2: ThinkingBox-Bench pass@1 (%) by domain. Each model is evaluated on every task for 20 repeated trials. Bold marks the group leader; underline marks the runner-up. The standard errors for the single attempt score estimates are provided in Table 4 in our ThinkingBox paper.

Claude Opus 5.5 leads overall at 67.16%, two-thirds of a point above Claude Opus 5. Kimi-K3 is the strongest open-weights model, within a point of GPT-6-Astra. Domain matters just as much: Claude Opus 4.6 scores 68.62% on retail but 8.30% on auto insurance.

One good run tells you a model can do the work. It does not tell you whether it will do it again. So run every task 20 times and ask how much of that score survives.

Figure 2: How much of each model's single-attempt score survives 20 repeats.

Industry observers note that only three hold on to most of their pass@1 scores: GPT-6 Astra retains 78% of its single-attempt rate, and Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Opus 5 each retain 71%. At the other end, GLM-5.1, Kimi-K2.6 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro each keep about 8%.

The gap between what a model can do once and what it does every time is the whole story.

Industry observers note that figure 3: Breadth and consistency pull apart. Twelve of the eighteen models are shown; six below 33% pass@1 are omitted for legibility.

In a recent development, kimi-K3 has the broadest coverage of any model we tested. It solves 93.89% of the benchmark at least once: 476 of 507 tasks. Only 31 tasks defeat it entirely, the lowest count in the field. On retail workflows it leads outright at 82.24% pass@1, ahead of every proprietary model.

Kimi-K3 is also among the least consistent. Just 68 of 507 tasks, 13.41%, succeed in all 20 attempts.

Industry observers note that claude Opus 5 inverts this. It solves fewer tasks at least once (79.09%; 106 defeat it entirely) but completes 47.53% of the benchmark on every single attempt.

It has been revealed that A newer model does not fix this. Claude Opus 5.5 scores higher than Claude Opus 5 on every-attempt average, 67.16% against 66.50%, and solves more tasks at least once. It passes exactly the same number of tasks on all 20 attempts: 241. Half a point of headline accuracy bought no additional dependability at all.

If you are choosing a model for work that touches real records, pass@20 is the wrong column to look at.

Industry observers note that capability comparisons usually stop at the score. For anyone deploying, the relevant question is what a successful unit of work costs. We measure that as cost per successful task attempt. We say task attempt because every benchmark task is run repeatedly and cost is incurred per attempt, so pass@1 is the matching quality denominator.

Sources indicate that we took each model's recorded token usage from its full 507 × 20 campaign and priced it at undiscounted list rates available on OpenRouter+, reversing promotional discounts and excluding endpoints that declare quantization. Input, output and cache rates all come from one provider endpoint per model.

Then we divided one run's cost by the number of attempts that succeeded:.

Cost per successful task attempt = estimated cost for 507 attempts, one per task ÷ (507 × pass@1).

This is a comparative efficiency index, not an invoice, and not the price of serving one production request. It also prices single successes, not consistency. We price consistency next.

Example: GPT-5.4 costs $43.49 for 507 attempts (one attempt per task) and has 65.36% pass@1, so $43.49 ÷ (507 × 0.6536) = $0.131 per successful task attempt.

A model is on the frontier if no other model is both no more expensive and at least as accurate. Three models qualify; every other model is dominated on at least one axis.

Figure 4: Cost per successful task attempt against pass@1. Ringed dots are pareto cost frontier models.

Recent findings suggest that the frontier has three steps. GPT-5.6 Sol has the lowest cost per success at $0.127; GPT-5.4 raises pass@1 by 3.45 percentage points for $0.004 more per success; Claude Opus 5.5 adds another 1.80 points at $0.276 per success. Each of the three remains on the cost frontier line because no cheaper model matches its pass@1.

Claude Opus 5 is the clearest case: at $0.475 per successful attempt and 66.50% pass@1, it is both more expensive and less accurate than Claude Opus 5.5 at $0.276 and 67.16%.

According to recent reports, cost per success rewards a model that is cheap and often right. It does not reward a model that is right every time. So we also compute cost per dependable task: the cost of the full 20-run campaign divided by the number of tasks the model passed on all 20 attempts.

Cost per dependable task = estimated cost of 20 runs of 507 attempts ÷ tasks passing 20/20.

Example: GPT-6-Astra costs 20 × $86.03 = $1,720.60 for the campaign and passes 231 tasks on every attempt, so $1,720.60 ÷ 231 = $7.45 per dependable task.

Table 3: The nine lowest costs per dependable task among models with at least one observed 20/20 task, sorted low to high. Estimated $, not actual cloud bills.

Industry observers note that now rank by consistency. GPT-5.4 is the cheapest at $6.80, though only 128 tasks meet the bar. GPT-6 Astra reaches 231 at $7.45, and Claude Opus 5.5 the joint-highest 241 at $7.80.

None of the three dominates the others: each additional dependable task costs more. Claude Opus 5 also passes 241, but at $13.30, so Opus 5.5 dominates it outright. GPT-5.6 Sol, the cheapest per single success at $0.127, costs $9.76 per dependable task. The cheapest way to get a right answer is not the cheapest way to get a dependable one.

We assign each failed trace one deterministic diagnostic signature, and the headline is actionable: roughly four in five failures are tool handling, not reasoning. Across an ablation study in Table 5 of our paper:.

These are unweighted averages of per-model shares and observable labels, not unique causal explanations.

The practical pattern is simple: agents usually get far enough to attempt the workflow, then fail to recover from tool errors, failed preconditions, or empty lookups. That is a retry and error-recovery problem before it is a model problem.

Difficulty also changes by domain: across the models listed in Table 2 above, retail averages 59.52% pass@1 while auto insurance averages 33.83%.

What to do about it. Treat the 20/20 rate as a design input, not a verdict. The same signal the benchmark grades on is available in production: check the terminal state before you commit, not the model's summary of it.

Classify tool and system errors so retries target the recoverable ones. Cut the tool surface to what the workflow needs. And require human approval on the changes you cannot cheaply reverse. We have not measured the lift from any of these on this benchmark, which is exactly the kind of thing the environment now makes testable.

ThinkingBox is the agent sandbox, while ThinkingBox-Bench is a dataset benchmark to evaluate agents. The diagram at the top of this post reveals the loop; here is what each part does.

Figure 5: The sandbox loop from panel A in Figure 1 above: isolated tool session, terminal database state, side effects, executable judges.

Recent findings suggest that each task defines a starting backend state, a user goal, the available MCP tools, the domain policy, and executable checks over the terminal state. A simulated user holds private context (a booking reference, a preference, or a date of birth) and releases it only when asked.

Industry observers note that every attempt gets an isolated MCP session with freshly initialized state. Two attempts of the same task never share a database row or cached tool state, which is what makes 20-trial comparison meaningful.

At the end, a side-effect extractor derives what actually changed, and deterministic judges compare it against the required end state, accepting any trajectory that produces the right outcome while rejecting wrong, missing or extra effects. For requirements with no clean database value ("did the agent disclose this is not guaranteed?"), a narrow binary rubric question handles the semantics. 477 of the 507 tasks are graded on state alone; 30 add response rubrics.

The trust boundary: the model sees tasks, dialogue and tool schemas. Golden state, assertions, grading internals and credentials stay on the evaluator side.

ThinkingBox is now on Hugging Face, both the harness and the dataset. ThinkingBox-Bench now sits behind the OpenEnv interface, and each finished episode returns a binary pass/fail reward. The released adapter is designed for evaluation; separate, non-benchmark scenarios can use the same interface in training workflows.

It has been revealed that tested on Linux and WSL, with Python 3.11+, uv and Docker. You also need a thinkingbox-data checkout at the pinned release and model endpoints for the agent, simulated user and judge. One endpoint can serve all three roles, which is the simplest way to start. The OpenEnv image starts only the OpenEnv API; everything else you run yourself.

In a second terminal, start Typesense 30.1 and wait for its health check:.

In a third terminal, start the Session Proxy and MCP servers.

Back in the first terminal, start the OpenEnv server against a ThinkingBox YAML config naming your three models (config guide):.

Sources indicate that gate on readiness before running anything. It returns 503 until its observable data, configuration and Session Proxy checks pass. It cannot observe Typesense or live-probe every model endpoint, so confirm those separately:.

According to recent reports, now score a real episode. example_usage.py only resets and lists tools; for agent actions, effects and assertions use the packaged evaluator:.

The OpenEnv adapter writes operational failures to an errors sidecar so they can be rerun rather than silently mixed with model outcomes. A canonical result must resolve or explicitly account for those attempts; we counted system errors as unsuccessful trials.

Runs are gated on a pinned framework commit, a pinned data release and a bundle hash, so a canonical result is verifiable rather than asserted.

According to recent reports, the useful part of this work is not our pass@1 leaderboard. It is the environment.

If you are evaluating an agent that touches real records:.

ThinkingBox code is MIT-licensed; the benchmark data is CDLA-Permissive-2.0; the OpenEnv environment ships under OpenEnv's BSD-3-Clause.

Sources indicate that disclaimer: every task in the public benchmark is a synthetic reconstruction. The workflows and policies are modeled on real AI agentic enterprise patterns; the customers are not real.

It has been revealed that thinkingBox and ThinkingBox-Bench is built by the Microsoft Copilot Studio team in partnership with Toloka with collaborators from the University of Pittsburgh, Northwestern University, Columbia University and UC Irvine who interned at Microsoft. Questions are welcome in the comments section below or on github or by email at firstnamelastname@microsoft.com.

Sources indicate that ST003_006 delegates its pass check to validate_database. Unequal result and golden database hashes fail even when diff is empty. The diff explains a failure; it does not decide the pass.

According to recent reports, this small replay exercises the released function with four authored effect inputs. Run python3 reproduce.py. It verifies the source pin and tests supplied hashes; it does not calculate a database hash, run an agent, or reproduce the full environment.

AI-assisted source reading and example by CyberNative AI LLC.

The useful cut is agent-reported "done" versus backend terminal state.

Recent findings suggest that A green success from the same process that acted is a claim, not a grade. I'd want the eval to score durable side effects (ticket status, refund state, policy-cited fields) against a frozen oracle — and fail when the narrative is green while the database disagrees.

Practical check: can a run be marked done when the terminal-state fixture is red?
